lesson.title: Expectations That Create Their Own Reality
lesson.summary: A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when an expectation about a person, even an inaccurate one, changes how others behave toward that person in ways that eventually make the expectation come true, most famously studied in classrooms by Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson.
lesson.body:
The term self-fulfilling prophecy was coined by sociologist Robert Merton in the late 1940s to describe situations where a false belief about a situation triggers behavior that makes the originally false belief come true. In psychology, the concept usually refers to interpersonal expectations specifically: if I expect you to behave a certain way, I may treat you differently because of that expectation, and my different treatment can actually shift how you behave, seemingly confirming that my original expectation was correct all along, even though the expectation is really what created the outcome rather than merely predicting it.

The most famous demonstration is the classroom study conducted by Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson, published as Pygmalion in the Classroom in 1968. Teachers were told that certain students in their classes, identified by a supposed test of academic potential, were likely to show unusual intellectual growth over the coming year. In reality, those students had been chosen at random and were no different from their classmates. Teachers, believing the label, appear to have treated those students somewhat differently, with subtle differences in warmth, attention, and the kind of feedback given, and by the end of the study period, the labeled students showed greater gains on later testing than their classmates, especially in the earlier grades.

This study deserves a fair, honest hedge. Since its publication, it has faced substantial methodological criticism, including questions about how the growth in test scores was measured and how large the true effect actually was, and later attempts to replicate the original findings at the same magnitude have had mixed results. Rosenthal went on to conduct many further studies and meta-analyses of what he called interpersonal expectancy effects across classrooms, workplaces, and other settings, and that broader body of work supports the idea that expectations really do shape behavior in a way that can become self-confirming, but the effects found across this larger literature tend to be more modest and inconsistent than the dramatic original Pygmalion study is often remembered as showing.

Self-fulfilling prophecy connects naturally to ideas already covered. It often works partly through the same mechanism behind the mere exposure effect, since a teacher who expects more from a student may unconsciously give that student more attention and more chances to interact, and that increased exposure itself can build warmer rapport. It also interacts with attribution: when an expected low achiever struggles, a teacher may attribute the struggle to fixed lack of ability rather than to a lack of encouragement, which only reinforces the original expectation and the unequal treatment behind it. Outside the classroom, the same loop plays out whenever we expect a first date to go badly and act a little cold without realizing it, then read the resulting awkwardness as proof we were right from the start.
